title: Damp and Mould Claims for Council Tenants | Housing Condition Claims UK
meta: Council tenant living with persistent damp or mould? Learn when your landlord may be responsible, what evidence to keep and how a housing claim may help.
h1: Damp and mould should not be part of your home.
intro: If your council or housing association has failed to address persistent damp, mould or the underlying repair problem, you may be entitled to seek repairs and compensation.
signsHeading: Signs of actionable damp and mould
signsIntro: Damp has different causes. A claim is strongest where the conditions arise from a repair defect, inadequate installations or a serious hazard the landlord should address.
signs: Black mould repeatedly returning after cleaning
Water staining, peeling paint or crumbling plaster
Penetrating damp from defective walls, roofs or windows
Condensation linked to inadequate heating or ventilation
Musty smells, damaged belongings or unusable rooms
Breathing problems or worsening health symptoms
duties: Landlords are commonly responsible for keeping the structure and exterior in repair, maintaining heating and water installations and ensuring rented homes remain fit for human habitation. They should identify and address the underlying cause rather than simply paint over visible mould.
councilHeading: Council landlords must take damp seriously.
council: Report damp and mould through the council repairs system and keep every reference number. Social landlords in England also have specific duties for prescribed hazards under Awaab’s Law, alongside their wider repairing and safety obligations.
evidence: Dated photographs showing each affected room
Repair reports, reference numbers and complaint responses
A timeline showing when the mould appeared and returned
Receipts for damaged belongings or extra heating costs
Medical records if the conditions affected health
Notes of inspections, appointments and missed visits
faqs: Can I claim if the council says the mould is condensation?
Possibly. The cause must be properly investigated. Condensation may be connected to inadequate heating, ventilation, insulation or another defect for which the landlord is responsible.
Should I keep cleaning the mould?
Take clear dated photographs before cleaning and follow reasonable safety advice. Cleaning visible mould does not remove the landlord’s duty to investigate an underlying defect.
What can compensation cover?
Depending on the evidence, compensation may reflect inconvenience, loss of use, damaged belongings, additional costs and proven injury. There is no fixed tariff.

title: Leaking Roof and Water Damage Claims | Council Tenants
meta: Help for council and housing association tenants affected by leaking roofs, pipes, ceilings or windows where reported repairs remain unresolved.
eyebrow: Council leak and water damage claims
h1: A recurring leak needs more than a temporary patch.
intro: Unresolved leaks can damage ceilings, walls, electrics and belongings. If your landlord knew about the problem but failed to complete an effective repair, we can assess your housing condition claim.
signsHeading: Water damage that should be investigated
signsIntro: The source of a leak is not always directly above the visible damage. Your landlord should investigate the cause and complete an effective repair.
signs: Water entering through a roof, wall or window
Recurring ceiling stains, bubbling paint or wet plaster
Leaking internal, communal or external pipework
Overflowing gutters or defective drainage
Mould developing around repeated water ingress
Water near light fittings, sockets or wiring
duties: A landlord’s repairing obligations commonly cover the structure and exterior, including roofs, drains, gutters and external pipes, together with installations for water and sanitation. Once notified, the landlord should investigate and act within a reasonable time.
councilHeading: Repeated jobs do not equal a completed repair.
council: If the council repeatedly closes repair jobs while water continues to enter, retain the job numbers and ask for the underlying cause to be recorded. Complaints, survey findings and photographs after rainfall can show that earlier work was ineffective.
evidence: Photos or videos during and after rainfall
Repair references and dates contractors attended
Copies of complaints and escalation responses
Receipts or photographs for damaged possessions
Evidence of unsafe electrics or unusable rooms
A diary of each recurrence and temporary repair
faqs: Can I claim for belongings damaged by a leak?
Documented losses may form part of a claim where legal responsibility is established. Keep photographs, receipts and evidence of the items’ condition and value.
What if the leak comes from another flat?
Responsibility depends on the source and who controls the relevant structure or pipework. The landlord should still investigate reports affecting your home.
Should I report every recurrence?
Yes. Reporting each recurrence creates a clear record that the repair was ineffective or the underlying cause remained unresolved.

title: Broken Heating and Hot Water Claims | Council Housing
meta: Council tenant left without reliable heating or hot water? Understand landlord duties, evidence and potential housing disrepair compensation.
eyebrow: Council heating and hot water claims
h1: Your home should be warm and have reliable hot water.
intro: Long or repeated periods without working heating or hot water can seriously affect daily life, particularly for children, older residents and people with health conditions.
signsHeading: Heating problems that may support a claim
signsIntro: The urgency and reasonable repair time depend on the season, household vulnerability, available alternatives and the nature of the fault.
signs: A boiler that repeatedly breaks down
No heating throughout the property
No reliable hot water for washing
Radiators or controls that do not work
Dangerous, leaking or condemned equipment
Temporary heaters supplied without a permanent repair
duties: Landlords are generally responsible for keeping installations for space heating and hot water in repair and proper working order. They must also consider whether the resulting cold or lack of facilities makes the home unsafe or unfit.
councilHeading: Make the council aware of vulnerability.
council: When reporting the failure, tell the council if children, elderly residents or anyone with a relevant medical condition lives at the property. Record any emergency heaters supplied, extra electricity used and every period without service.
evidence: Repair logs and boiler fault codes
Dates and duration of every loss of service
Messages showing household vulnerability
Receipts for heaters and additional energy costs
Contractor notes or gas safety information
Medical evidence where cold affected health
faqs: How quickly should heating be repaired?
There is no universal deadline for every fault, but a complete loss of heating in cold weather requires a much faster response than a minor non-urgent defect.
Can I claim extra electricity costs?
Reasonable, evidenced additional costs may be relevant. Keep bills and receipts showing use of temporary electric heaters.
What if the boiler keeps being reset?
Repeated temporary resets may show that the underlying fault has not been resolved. Continue reporting each failure and keep the repair references.

title: Pest Infestation Claims for Council Tenants | Housing Claims
meta: Information for council tenants affected by rats, mice, cockroaches or other pests entering through housing defects or unresolved communal problems.
h1: Pests entering through disrepair should not be ignored.
intro: Where rats, mice, cockroaches or other pests are linked to defects, drainage or communal conditions under the landlord’s control, the landlord may be responsible for putting the problem right.
signsHeading: When pests may be linked to disrepair
signsIntro: Responsibility is fact-specific. Evidence connecting the infestation to the building, communal areas or another landlord-controlled defect is particularly important.
signs: Holes or gaps in external walls and floors
Broken air bricks, drains or waste systems
Pests travelling through communal spaces
Repeated infestation despite appropriate treatment
Contaminated cupboards, surfaces or belongings
Droppings, nesting materials or gnaw damage
duties: A landlord may be responsible where an infestation results from disrepair, a structural entry point, defective drainage or conditions in communal areas under its control. Tenants should maintain reasonable cleanliness and cooperate with inspections and treatment.
councilHeading: Ask the council to inspect the entry points.
council: A pest-control visit alone may not solve the problem. Ask the council to record and repair holes, defective drains, communal refuse issues or other routes through which pests enter the property.
evidence: Photographs of pests, droppings and entry points
Pest-control reports identifying likely causes
Council repair and environmental health reports
Dates of treatments and repeat infestations
Receipts for cleaning or damaged belongings
Complaints from neighbouring tenants where relevant
faqs: Is my landlord always responsible for pests?
No. Responsibility depends on the cause. Claims are stronger where pests enter because of structural defects, drainage or communal conditions controlled by the landlord.
What if pest control keeps visiting?
Repeated treatment without sealing entry points may not be an effective remedy. Record every visit and continued signs of infestation.
Can communal problems support my case?
They may. Photographs, neighbour reports and records concerning communal bins, drains or shared areas can help establish the source.

title: Unsafe Electrics Housing Claims | Council Tenant Solicitors
meta: Help for council tenants dealing with exposed wiring, faulty sockets, water near electrics or other reported electrical hazards in rented homes.
intro: Faulty sockets, exposed wiring, repeated tripping or water near electrical fittings can place your household at risk. Report immediate danger promptly and avoid using affected equipment.
signsIntro: Do not touch exposed wiring or use equipment you believe is unsafe. Emergency risks should be reported through the landlord’s urgent repair route.
signs: Exposed, loose or damaged wiring
Sockets that spark, overheat or show burn marks
Repeated loss of power or tripping circuits
Water leaking near lights or sockets
Broken switches or electrical fittings
Contractor advice that an installation is unsafe
duties: Landlords must keep relevant electrical installations in repair and ensure rented accommodation is safe. The appropriate response depends on the hazard, but immediate risks should not be left awaiting routine repair times.
councilHeading: Use the emergency repair route for immediate danger.
council: Tell the council clearly if there is sparking, burning, exposed wiring or water near electrics. Keep the call reference and, once safe, follow up in writing so there is a permanent record.
evidence: Safe photographs of the visible defect
Emergency repair and out-of-hours references
Electrician or contractor reports
Dates power or facilities were unavailable
Evidence of damaged appliances or belongings
Medical or fire-service records where relevant
faqs: What should I do if electrics are sparking?
Keep away from the hazard, stop using affected equipment and contact the landlord’s emergency repairs service. Call the emergency services where there is an immediate threat to life or fire.
Can a water leak become an electrical claim?
Potentially. Water near wiring, sockets or light fittings can create a separate safety hazard requiring urgent investigation.
Should I arrange my own electrician?
Seek advice before commissioning work or deducting costs from rent, except where emergency safety action is unavoidable. Keep all records and receipts.

title: Structural Damage and Cracks Claims | Council Housing
meta: Council housing claims involving serious cracks, unstable ceilings, damaged floors, subsidence indicators and unresolved structural defects.
h1: Serious cracks and movement deserve a proper investigation.
intro: Not every crack indicates structural failure, but widening cracks, movement, unstable surfaces or falling material should be inspected rather than repeatedly filled or painted over.
signsIntro: A qualified inspection may be necessary to distinguish cosmetic movement from a defect affecting the structure, safety or use of the home.
signs: Large, widening or stepped cracks
Cracks repeatedly reopening after repair
Sagging or unstable ceilings
Uneven, damaged or collapsing floors
Doors and windows suddenly sticking
Falling plaster, masonry or external render
duties: Landlords are commonly responsible for keeping the structure and exterior in repair. Where reported cracking or movement may indicate a safety issue, the landlord should investigate the cause and complete appropriate remedial work.
councilHeading: Ask for the defect—not just the decoration—to be assessed.
council: If contractors repeatedly fill cracks without explaining why they return, ask the council to escalate the matter for a technical inspection. Photograph the cracks beside a ruler and record changes over time.
evidence: Dated photographs showing width and progression
Surveyor, contractor or building-control reports
Repair records for previous patch work
Videos of movement or falling material
Details of rooms or facilities affected
Records of any temporary relocation
faqs: Are all cracks housing disrepair?
No. Fine cosmetic cracking may not amount to actionable disrepair. Size, progression, cause, safety and the landlord’s response all matter.
What if the council keeps filling the crack?
Repeated cosmetic work may be inadequate if an underlying structural or moisture-related cause remains. Keep records showing recurrence.
Can I request a survey?
You can ask the landlord to arrange an appropriate inspection. Independent expert evidence may later be required depending on the claim.

title: Council Housing Disrepair Claims | Specialist Tenant Solicitors
meta: Specialist help for council tenants whose landlord has failed to repair damp, mould, leaks, heating, pests, unsafe electrics or structural damage.
h1: When the council fails to repair your home, you still have rights.
intro: Council tenants should have a safe, habitable home. If repeated repair reports and complaints have not resolved serious conditions, our specialist team can assess a claim for repairs and compensation.
signsHeading: Problems we help council tenants address
signsIntro: Claims depend on the defect, notice, reasonable repair time and evidence. More than one issue can form part of the same housing condition claim.
signs: Persistent damp, mould or condensation hazards
Leaking roofs, pipes, ceilings or windows
Broken boilers, heating or hot water
Pests linked to structural or communal defects
Unsafe electrical installations
Cracks, damaged floors or unstable ceilings
duties: Councils have repairing obligations under tenancy and housing law, including duties concerning the structure and exterior, key installations and fitness for human habitation. Separate complaint, ombudsman and enforcement routes may also be available.
councilHeading: A closed repair job does not close the problem.
council: Keep reporting unresolved or recurring defects even if the council marks a job complete. Use the formal complaints process where necessary and retain every reference, response, appointment and photograph.
evidence: A full timeline of reports and complaints
Repair references and contractor appointments
Photographs and videos of every affected area
Council inspection or survey records
Medical evidence and household vulnerability
Receipts for damaged belongings and extra costs
faqs: Can I claim against my local council?
Potentially, where the council is your landlord, is legally responsible for the conditions and failed to act within a reasonable time after notice.
Must I complete the council complaint process first?
Not always, but complaints can help clarify the council’s position and create valuable evidence. The correct route depends on your circumstances.
Could making a claim affect my tenancy?
Tenants are entitled to report disrepair and seek advice. Continue complying with your tenancy, including paying rent, while the matter is addressed.

title: Housing Association Disrepair Claims | Tenant Solicitors
meta: Housing association tenant facing unresolved damp, leaks, heating failures or unsafe conditions? Learn about repairs, evidence and potential compensation.
h1: Your housing association must take reported disrepair seriously.
intro: Housing association tenants have legal protections concerning repairs and the condition of their homes. Repeated delays, ineffective work or closed jobs may justify further action.
signsHeading: Conditions that may support a claim
signsIntro: The central questions are usually whether the landlord was responsible, knew about the problem and had a reasonable opportunity to put it right.
signs: Damp, mould or excessive cold
Roof, pipe, window or drainage leaks
Broken heating or hot-water installations
Pests entering through defects
Unsafe sockets, wiring or fittings
Structural cracking or damaged surfaces
duties: Housing associations are social landlords and commonly have duties concerning repairs, safety and fitness for human habitation. Their published repair standards and complaints process may provide additional evidence about expected response times.
councilHeading: Social landlord records can be valuable evidence.
council: Keep portal screenshots, repair references, complaint responses and contractor messages. If a job disappears from the system or is marked complete, photograph the unresolved defect and report it again in writing.
evidence: Screenshots from the repairs portal
Emails, texts and complaint decisions
Dated photographs of recurring defects
Contractor attendance and no-access records
Records of vulnerabilities and health impacts
Receipts for property damage or extra costs
faqs: Can I claim against a housing association?
Potentially. Housing associations have repairing and safety duties. A claim depends on responsibility, notice, reasonable repair time and supporting evidence.
What if repairs are repeatedly cancelled?
Keep every cancellation message and appointment record. Repeated failed visits can help demonstrate delay, although the full circumstances must be considered.
Can I also contact the Housing Ombudsman?
The Ombudsman and a legal claim serve different purposes. Depending on the circumstances, one or both routes may be appropriate.
